source_text: Nam et orandi perseuerantiam et instantiam mandans parabolam iudicis ponit coacti audire uiduam instantia et perseuerantia interpellationum eius. ergo iudicem deum ostendit orandum, non se, si non ipse est iudex. sed (et) subiunxit facturum deum uindictam electorum suorum. si ergo ipse erit uindex qui et iudex, [si] creatorem ergo meliorem deum probauit, quem electorum suorum clamantium ad eum die et nocte uindicem ostendit. et tamen, cum templum creatoris inducit et duos adorantes diuersa mente describit, Pharisaeum in superbia, publicanum in humilitate, ideoque alterum reprobatum, alterum iustificatum descendisse, utique docendo, qua disciplina sit orandum, eum et hic orandum constituit, a quo relaturi essent iam orandi. disciplinam, siue reprobatricem superbiae siue iustificatricem humilitatis. alterius dei nec templum nec oratores nec iudicium inuenio penes Christum, nisi creatoris: illum iubet adorare in humilitate, ut adleuatorem hurnilium, non in superbia, ut destructorem superborum. quem alium adorandum mihi ostendit? qua disciplina? qua spe? neminem, opinor. nam et quam docuit orationem creatori probauimus conuenire. aliud est, si etiam adorari, qua deus optimus et ultro bonus, non uult. \'Sed quis optimus nisi unus, inquit, deus\'? non quasi ex duobus diis unum optimum ostenderit, sed (unum) esse optimum deum solum, qui sic unus sit optimus, qua solus deus. et utique optimus qui pluit super iustos et iniustos et solem suum oriri facit super bonos et malos, sustinens et alens et iuuans etiam Marcionitas. Denique interrogatus ab illo quodam: praeceptor optime, quid faciens uitam aeternam possidebo? de praeceptis creatoris an ea sciret, id est faceret, expostulauit, ad contestandum praeceptis creatoris uitam adquiri sempiternam, cumque ille principaliora quaeque adfirmasset obseruasse se ab adolescentia: unum, inquit, tibi deest: omnia, quaecumque habes, uende et da pauperibus. et habebis thesaurum in caelo, et ueni, sequere me. age, Marcion, omnesque iam \'commiserones* et \'coodibiles\' eius, haeretici, quid audebitis dicere? resciditne Christus priora praecepta non occidendi non adulterandi non furandi non falsum testandi diligendi patrem et matrem, an et illa seruauit et quod deerat adiecit, — quamquam et hoc praeceptum largitionis in egenos ubique diffusum sit in lege et prophetis — uti gloriosissimus ille obseruator praeceptorum pecuniam multo cariorem habiturus traduceretur? saluum eat igitur et hic euangelio: non ueni dissoluere legem et prophetas, sed potius adimplere. simul et cetera dubitatione liberauit manifestando unius esse et \'dei\' nomen et (optimi), et uitam aeternam\' et \'thesaurum in caelo\', et semetipsum cuius praecepta supplendo et conseruauit et auxit, secundum Micheam quoque hoc loco recognoscendus dicentem: si adnuntiauit tibi homo, quid bonum? aut quid a te dominus exquirit quam facere iudicium diligere misericordiam et paratum esse sequi dominum deum tuum? et <homo\' enim Christus adnuntians, quid sit bonum: scientiam legis: praecepta, inquit, scis; \'facere iudicium\': uende, inquit, quae habes; \'diligere misericordiam\': et da, inquit, egenis; «paratum esse [inquitj ire cum domino\': et ueni, inquit, sequere me. Tam distincta fuit a primordio Iudaea gens per tribus et populos et familias et domos, ut nemo facile ignorari de genere potuisset, uel de recentibus Augustianis censibus adhuc tunc fortasse pendentibus. Iesus autem Marcionis, — et (si) natus non dubitaretur qui homo uidebatur - utique, qua non natus, nullam potuerat generis sui in publico habuisse notitiam, sed erat unus aliqui deputandus ex his, qui quo(quo) modo ignoti habebantur. cum igitur praetereuntem illum caecus audisset, cur exclamauit: Iesu, fili Dauid, miserere mei, nisi quia filius Dauid, (id) est ex familia Dauid, non temere deputabatur per matrem et fratres, qui aliquando, ex notitia utique, adnuntiati ei fuerant? (sed antecedentes increpabant caecum, uti taceret\'. merito, quoniam quidem uociferabatur, non quia de Dauid filio mentiebatur. aut doce increpantes illos scisse, quod Iesus non esset filius Dauid, ut idcirco silentium caeco indixisse credantur. sed et si doceres. facilius illos ignorasse praesumeres quam dominum falsam in se praedicationem sustinere potuisse. \'sed patiens dominus\'. non tamen confirmator erroris. immo etiam detector creatoris ut non prius hanc caecitatem hominis illius enubilasset, ne ultra Iesum filium Dauid existimaret? atquin, ne patientiam eius infamaretis nec ullam rationem dissimulationis illi adfigeretis, [ne filium Dauid negaretis manifestissime confirmauit caeci praedicationem et ipsa remuneratione medicinae et testimonio fidei: fides, inquit, tua te saluum fecit. quid uis caecum credidisse? ab alio deo descendisse Iesum ad detectionem creatoris, ad destructionem legis et prophetarum? non illum esse, qui ex radice Iesse et ex fructu lumborum Dauid destinabatur, caecorum quoque remunerator? sed nondum, puto, eiusmodi tunc caeci erant qualis Marcion, ut haec fuerit caeci illius fides, qua crediderit in uoce: Iesu, fili Dauid. qui hoc se et cognouit et cognosci ab omnibus uoluit I fidem hominis, etsi melius oculatam, etsi ueri luminis compotem, exteriore quoque uisione donauit, ut et nos regulam simulque mercedem fidei disceremus: qui uult uidere. Iesum Dauid filium credat per uirginis censum; qui non ita credet, non audiet ab illo: fides tua te saluum fecit, atque ita caecus remanebit, ruens in antithesin, ruentem et ipsam (in) antithesin. sic enim caecus caecum deducere solet. nam si, (quia) aliquando Dauid in recuperatione Sionis offenderant caeci, resistentes quominus admitteretur, — in figuram populi proinde caeci, non admissuri quandoque Christum filium Dauid — ideo Christus ex diuerso caeco subuenit, ut hinc se ostenderet non esse filium Dauid, ut ex animi diuersitate bonus caecis, quos ille iusserat caedi, id cur fidei et quidem prauae praestitisse se dixit? atquin et hoc (filius Dauid\' (dat) antithesin de suo retundendam. nam quia Dauid offenderant caeci, nunc uero eiusdem t carnis homo supplicem se obtulerat filio Dauid, idcirco ei satisfacienti quodammodo placatus filius Dauid restituit lumina cum testimonio fidei, qua hoc ipsum crediderat exorandum sibi esse filium Dauid. et tamen Dauid audacia hominum, puto, offenderat, non ualitudo.
pass_a_gloss: For He commands perseverance and insistence in prayer, setting forth a parable of a judge, forced to hear a widow by her insistence and perseverance in her petitions. Therefore, He shows that God is to be prayed to, not Himself, if He is not the judge. But He also added that God will execute vengeance for His elect. If, then, He will be the avenger who is also the judge, He has proved the Creator to be the better God, whom He shows to be the avenger of His elect, who cry out to Him day and night. And yet, when He introduces the temple of the Creator and describes two people worshiping with different minds, a Pharisee in pride and a publican in humility, and therefore one is rejected and the other justified, He is teaching by what discipline one ought to pray, and He establishes that one ought to pray to Him from whom they will receive the reward of their prayer, whether it is a discipline that reproves pride or justifies humility. I do not find the temple or worshipers or judgment of another God with Christ, except that of the Creator: He commands to worship in humility, as the helper of the humble, not in pride, as the destroyer of the proud. Who else does He show me to worship? By what discipline? By what hope? No one, I think. For He also taught a prayer that we have approved as suitable for the Creator. It is different if He also does not want to be worshiped, as the best and kindest God. 'But who is the best God, except the one God?' He does not show one God to be the best out of two, but that the one God is the best, who is the only God, and certainly the best, who rains on the just and the unjust and makes His sun rise over the good and the evil, sustaining and nourishing and helping even the Marcionites. Finally, when asked by a certain man, 'Good Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' He inquired whether he knew the commandments of the Creator, that is, whether he did them, in order to testify that eternal life is acquired by the commandments of the Creator. And when the man had affirmed that he had observed the principal commandments from his youth, He said, 'One thing you still lack: sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me.' Come, Marcion, and all you who are now 'co-miserable' and 'co-odious' with him, heretics, what will you dare to say? Did Christ abolish the former commandments, 'Do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor your father and mother,' or did He also keep those and add what was lacking? — although this commandment of giving to the poor is also diffused everywhere in the law and the prophets — so that the most glorious observer of the commandments, having much more precious money, would be betrayed? Let him go, then, and this Gospel: 'I did not come to destroy the law and the prophets, but to fulfill them.' At the same time, He freed the other doubts, manifesting that the name 'God' and 'best' and 'eternal life' and 'treasure in heaven' belong to one, and that He Himself, whose commandments He was supplementing and conserving and increasing, is the one according to Micah, who is recognized in this place as saying: 'If a man has announced to you what is good, or what does the Lord require of you, except to do justice, to love mercy, and to be prepared to follow the Lord your God?' And Christ, announcing what is good, says, 'You know the commandments'; 'to do justice,' He says, 'sell what you have'; 'to love mercy,' He says, 'and give to the poor'; 'to be prepared to follow the Lord,' He says, 'and come, follow me.' The Jewish people were so distinct from the beginning, divided into tribes and peoples and families and houses, that no one could easily be ignorant of their kind or family, even from the recent Augustan censuses, which were perhaps still pending at that time. But Jesus, according to Marcion, — and if He was not born, it would not be doubted who He seemed to be — certainly, since He was not born, He could not have had any public knowledge of His kind, but He would have been considered one of those who were unknown in some way. When, therefore, a blind man heard Him passing by, why did he cry out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me,' unless He was not rashly considered the Son of David, that is, from the family of David, through His mother and brothers, who had at some point been announced to him, as it were, from knowledge? But those who came before rebuked the blind man, that he should be silent. Rightly so, since he was crying out, not because he was lying about being the Son of David. Or do you teach that those who rebuked him knew that Jesus was not the Son of David, so that they are believed to have imposed silence on the blind man for that reason? But even if you teach this, it is easier to presume that they were ignorant than that the Lord could have endured a false proclamation about Himself. 'But the Lord is patient.' Nevertheless, He is not a confirmer of error. On the contrary, He is also the detector of the Creator, so that He did not previously dispel the blindness of that man, lest he think that Jesus is the Son of David. But, lest you defame His patience or attach any reason for dissimulation to Him, He clearly confirmed the blind man's proclamation, both by the reward of the healing and by the testimony of faith: 'Your faith has saved you.' What do you want the blind man to have believed? That Jesus came down from another God to detect the Creator, to destroy the law and the prophets? Is He not the one who was destined from the root of Jesse and from the fruit of the loins of David, the rewarder of the blind? But, I think, the blind men were not of such a kind at that time as Marcion, so that the faith of that blind man was that he believed in the voice: 'Jesus, Son of David.' Who recognized Himself and wanted to be recognized by all, gave faith to the man, even if it was better to have the eyes open, even if it was to have the true light, He also gave it by external vision, so that we might learn the rule and reward of faith at the same time: whoever wants to see, let him believe that Jesus is the Son of David through the census of the Virgin; whoever does not believe in this way will not hear from Him: 'Your faith has saved you,' and thus the blind man will remain, falling into heresy, and heresy itself will fall into heresy. For the blind are accustomed to lead the blind. For if, because the blind had at some point offended David in the recovery of Zion, resisting so that he would not be admitted, — in figure, therefore, the blind people, who would not admit Christ the Son of David — therefore Christ helps the blind man in a different way, so that He shows Himself not to be the Son of David, as if, from a diversity of mind, He is good to the blind, whom He had ordered to be killed, why did He say that He had endured false faith? But, on the contrary, this 'Son of David' also gives heresy to be refuted from His own. For since the blind had offended David, now, indeed, a man of the same flesh offered Himself as a suppliant to the Son of David, and therefore, placated, the Son of David restored his sight, with the testimony of faith, by which he had believed that he had to pray for the Son of David. And yet David had offended the audacity of men, I think, not their strength.

pass_b_english: He commands perseverance and insistence in prayer, illustrating it with a parable: a judge forced to hear a widow because of her insistence and perseverance in her petitions. So He shows that God is to be prayed to, not Himself—unless He Himself is the judge. He also adds that God will execute vengeance for His elect. If, then, He will be the Avenger who is also the Judge, He has proved the Creator to be the better God—the One He shows as the Avenger of His elect crying out to Him day and night. And yet, when He introduces the Creator's temple and describes two worshipers with different minds—a Pharisee in pride, a tax collector in humility—with the result that one is rejected and the other justified, He is teaching by what discipline one ought to pray. He establishes that one must pray to the One from whom they will receive the reward of their prayer, whether that discipline reproves pride or justifies humility. I find no temple, no worshipers, no judgment of another God with Christ—except the Creator's. He commands worship in humility, as the helper of the humble, not in pride, as the destroyer of the proud. Who else does He show me to worship? By what discipline? By what hope? No one, I think. For we have also approved the prayer He taught as suitable for the Creator. It would be different if even the best and kindest God does not want to be worshiped. 'But who is best except the one God?' He does not show one God to be the best out of two; He shows that the one God is the Best, who is the only God—and certainly the Best, who rains on the just and the unjust and makes His sun rise on the good and the evil (Matthew 5:45), sustaining and nourishing and helping even the Marcionites.

Finally, when a certain man asked, 'Good Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?' Jesus inquired whether he knew the commandments of the Creator—that is, whether he did them—in order to testify that eternal life is acquired by the Creator's commandments. When the man affirmed he had kept the principal ones from youth, Jesus said, 'One thing you still lack: sell all you have, give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.' Come now, Marcion, and all you 'co-miserable' and 'co-odious' heretics with him—what will you dare to say? Did Christ abolish the former commandments—do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, honor father and mother—or did He keep those and add what was lacking?—although this commandment of giving to the needy is also diffused everywhere in the Law and the Prophets—so that the most glorious observer of the commandments, who valued money much more, would be betrayed? Let this Gospel stand, then: 'I did not come to destroy the Law and the Prophets, but to fulfill them.' At the same time, He freed the other doubts, manifesting that the name 'God' and 'Best' and 'eternal life' and 'treasure in heaven' belong to one and the same, and that He Himself—whose commandments He was supplementing, conserving, and increasing—is the One recognized in Micah as saying: 'If a man has announced to you what is good, or what does the Lord require of you, except to do justice, to love mercy, and to be prepared to follow the Lord your God?' (Micah 6:8). And Christ, announcing what is good, says: 'You know the commandments'; 'to do justice,' He says, 'sell what you have'; 'to love mercy,' He says, 'and give to the poor'; 'to be prepared to follow the Lord,' He says, 'and come, follow me.'

The Jewish people were so distinct from the beginning—divided into tribes, peoples, families, and houses—that no one could easily be ignorant of their kind or family, even from the recent Augustan censuses, perhaps still pending at that time. But Marcion's Jesus—though, if He were not born, it would not be doubted that He seemed a man—certainly, since He was not born, He could have had no public knowledge of His lineage; He would have been reckoned as one of those unknown in some way. When a blind man heard Him passing by, why did he cry out, 'Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me,' unless He was not rashly considered the Son of David—that is, from the family of David—through His mother and brothers, who had at some point been made known to him from knowledge? Those going before rebuked the blind man to silence. Rightly so, since he was crying out—not because he was lying about being the Son of David. Or do you teach that the rebukers knew Jesus was not the Son of David, so they imposed silence for that reason? But even if you taught that, it is easier to presume they were ignorant than that the Lord could have endured a false proclamation about Himself. 'But the Lord is patient.' Nevertheless, He is not a confirmer of error. On the contrary, He is also the detector of the Creator—so that He did not previously dispel that man's blindness, lest he think Jesus the Son of David? But lest you defame His patience or attach any reason for dissimulation to Him, He clearly confirmed the blind man's proclamation—both by the reward of the healing and by the testimony of faith: 'Your faith has saved you.' What do you want the blind man to have believed? That Jesus came down from another God to detect the Creator, to destroy the Law and the Prophets? Is He not the One destined from the root of Jesse and the fruit of David's loins, the rewarder of the blind? But, I think, the blind men were not yet of such a kind as Marcion, so that the faith of that blind man was simply that he believed in the voice: 'Jesus, Son of David.' The One who recognized Himself and wanted to be recognized by all gave the man faith—even if better sighted, even if possessing true light—He also gave it by external vision, so that we might learn the rule and reward of faith at once: whoever wants to see, let him believe Jesus is the Son of David through the Virgin's census; whoever does not believe this way will not hear from Him, 'Your faith has saved you,' and thus the blind man will remain, falling into heresy, and heresy itself will fall into heresy. For the blind are accustomed to lead the blind.

For if the blind had once offended David in the recovery of Zion, resisting his admission—in figure, therefore, the blind people who would not admit Christ the Son of David—therefore Christ helped the blind man from the opposite direction, to show Himself not to be the Son of David? As if, from a diversity of mind, He is good to the blind whom He had ordered to be killed—why did He say He endured false faith? But on the contrary, this 'Son of David' also gives heresy to be refuted from His own. For since the blind had offended David, now a man of the same flesh offered himself as a suppliant to the Son of David; and therefore, placated, the Son of David restored his sight, with the testimony of faith by which he had believed he must pray to the Son of David. And yet David was offended by the audacity of men, I think, not their infirmity.
